articles.title: Airtel Money goes public in London, bringing Africa’s mobile money opportunity to global investors - TechTrendsKE
articles.summary: Airtel Money goes public in London, bringing Africa’s mobile money opportunity to global investors  TechTrendsKE
articles.full_text:
Airtel Money began conditional trading on the London Stock Exchange on Friday, 9 October, with an implied valuation of £5.3 billion, or about US$7 billion, giving investors a public-market route into one of Africa’s largest mobile money businesses.
The shares were priced at £1.96 each. They opened around that level and rose as high as £2 during early trading, a gain of about 2%, after the offering attracted demand several times greater than the number of shares available. The company’s formal admission to the exchange and the start of unconditional trading are expected on 14 October.
The listing gives Airtel Money a standalone market valuation as it seeks to expand beyond wallet transfers and mobile payments into a wider range of financial services. Its prospects will depend on how effectively it converts its large customer base and transaction volumes into revenue, while expanding digital adoption and merchant payments across its African markets.
Airtel Money shares begin trading in London
The offer price of £1.96 values Airtel Money at approximately £5.3 billion. The initial sale covers 270 million existing shares, with proceeds of about £529 million going to selling shareholders rather than being raised as new capital by the company. An additional 27 million shares may be sold through an over-allotment option. If exercised in full, that would increase the total offer to £582 million.
Airtel Africa is expected to remain a long-term strategic shareholder and retain control of Airtel Money. The listing therefore gives some existing investors an opportunity to sell shares while leaving the mobile money business under its parent group’s influence. The transaction is a secondary share sale, so Airtel Money does not receive the proceeds from the shares sold in the IPO.
The International Finance Corporation, the World Bank Group institution focused on private-sector development, was allocated shares worth £67.2 million under its cornerstone investment commitment. The offer also included an allocation of eight million shares for eligible UK retail investors. Conditional trading is initially restricted to investors who applied for and received shares in the offer, with broader unconditional trading expected to begin after formal admission.
Revenue and earnings give investors a measure of scale
Airtel Money’s valuation rests on an established business with substantial revenue and earnings. For the financial year ended March 2026, the company reported revenue of US$1.355 billion, up 36% from US$994 million a year earlier. Underlying EBITDA, a measure of operating earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, rose 31% to US$689 million. Its underlying EBITDA margin was 50.8%, down from 52.8% in the previous year.
The figures show both the pace of growth and the importance of maintaining profitability as the business expands. Wallet services generated US$648 million in revenue during the year, while payments and transfers contributed US$573 million. Financial services, including offerings such as credit and other financial products, generated US$61 million. These figures indicate that the business remains heavily reliant on core wallet and payment activity, even as it develops additional services.
The company’s transaction volumes have also grown beyond the scale of a conventional person-to-person transfer service. Airtel Money processed about US$213 billion in payments during the 12 months to June 2026, according to figures disclosed for the listing. That figure covers a different reporting period from the financial year ended March 2026, so it should not be directly compared with the full-year revenue figures. The volume nevertheless illustrates the breadth of activity moving through its network.
App adoption offers room to increase customer value
A key growth opportunity is encouraging more customers to use Airtel Money’s smartphone app and digital services. In the six markets highlighted in its IPO disclosures, app customers generated average revenue per user of about US$9.50, compared with US$1.80 among feature-phone customers. The figures suggest that customers using the app can be more valuable to the business, although the comparison does not establish that app usage alone accounts for the difference.
Smartphone users represented about half of Airtel Money’s customer base, but only around 13% of those smartphone customers used the app during the 12 months to June 2026. Airtel Money therefore has room to encourage existing customers to use more of its digital services rather than relying solely on basic wallet functions. The company’s disclosed app transaction value increased from about US$5.5 billion to US$10.95 billion over the period, showing a rise in activity through that channel.
For Airtel Money, higher app adoption could support greater use of payments, transfers and other services. It could also help the company build more frequent customer relationships and lower its dependence on physical agents for some transactions. The commercial outcome will depend on whether customers adopt these services at scale and whether the additional activity produces lasting revenue growth without eroding margins.
Merchant payments and financial services broaden the business
Merchant payments and bill payments are another important part of the company’s expansion. According to figures cited in coverage of the listing, revenue from these services increased by 61% in the 12 months to June 2026. More merchant transactions can give customers additional reasons to keep money in their wallets and use Airtel Money for everyday purchases, while providing businesses with a digital channel to receive payments.
Airtel Money’s network includes about 2.3 million agents and 490,000 merchants, alongside bank integrations and partners connected through its platforms. These relationships extend its reach beyond direct transfers between individuals and create opportunities to support retail payments, bill settlement and business transactions. The scale of the network is an advantage, but the value it generates depends on active usage, transaction economics and the ability to compete for merchant acceptance.
The company is also developing services that sit alongside payments, including credit, savings, insurance and other financial products in selected markets. A planned Mastercard virtual card is another route to connecting wallet balances with online and card-based payments. Such services could increase the number of ways customers use Airtel Money, although product availability and uptake will differ by market and remain important factors in assessing their contribution to earnings.
Competition and customer conversion will shape growth
Airtel Money operates in markets where mobile money is already an established part of daily financial life. In Kenya, it competes with Safaricom’s M-PESA, which has a broad merchant network and a strong position in consumer payments. Other markets also have local payment providers, banks and fintech companies seeking customers and transaction volume. Airtel Money’s opportunity is therefore not simply to add users, but to persuade consumers and businesses to make it a regular payment option.
The company’s existing telecommunications customer base offers a potential route to growth because some Airtel subscribers in its markets do not yet use Airtel Money. Converting those customers into active wallet users could expand its reach without requiring it to acquire every customer from outside the group. However, mobile connectivity and mobile money adoption are different measures, and the number of subscribers does not automatically translate into a comparable number of potential active wallet users.
In Kenya, Airtel Money has also been working to improve the proposition for merchants and consumers through bank integrations, cross-network transactions and initiatives such as Bizna Wallet. These efforts are relevant to its wider strategy because a wallet becomes more useful when customers can pay more merchants, move funds across services and use it for routine financial needs. Their long-term impact will depend on adoption and sustained transaction activity rather than the launch of individual features.
What the listing means for African fintech
Airtel Money’s London listing gives public-market investors a way to assess the financial performance of a large African digital payments business separately from its telecommunications parent. The valuation will be measured against revenue growth, profitability, customer activity and the company’s ability to extend its services beyond basic wallet transactions. Its early share-price movement provides an initial market reference, but conditional trading is not the same as a settled long-term valuation.
The offering also highlights the structure of the transaction. Because the IPO mainly involves existing shares, it provides liquidity for selling investors rather than a direct injection of new funds into Airtel Money. Airtel Africa’s continued majority ownership leaves the business connected to the wider group while it operates as an independently listed company.
For African fintech, the listing offers a public-market reference point for a business built on mobile money at continental scale. Airtel Money has substantial revenue, a large customer base and high transaction volumes, but its next period of growth will depend on whether it can convert those advantages into more frequent app usage, stronger merchant payments and broader financial-service adoption. Investors will be watching whether that expansion can continue while the company protects its earnings margins and competes in markets where customers already have established alternatives.

articles.title: Tipper Truck Market Forecast to 2035: Infrastructure and Mining Demand Drive Growth - News and Statistics - IndexBox
articles.summary: Tipper Truck Market Forecast to 2035: Infrastructure and Mining Demand Drive Growth - News and Statistics  IndexBox
articles.full_text:
Caterpillar Inc.
Leading in large mining trucks
According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Tipper Truck market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture.
The global tipper truck market is a vital segment of the commercial vehicle and heavy machinery industry, closely tied to infrastructure development, mining output, and construction spending. As of 2026, the market is shaped by cyclical demand from core end-use sectors, tightening emissions and safety regulations, and intensifying competition in powertrain technology and automation. This report provides a data-driven analysis of the world tipper truck market, covering historical performance from 2012 to 2025 and forecasting to 2035. It examines demand drivers, supply chain dynamics, trade flows, and pricing mechanisms.
The competitive landscape is assessed, profiling leading OEMs and regional players. The outlook synthesizes these findings to offer actionable insights for manufacturers, suppliers, investors, and policymakers navigating the next decade. The market is projected to grow at a moderate pace, with Asia-Pacific remaining the largest consumer, while North America and Europe see replacement demand and technological upgrades. Key trends include the shift toward electric and autonomous tippers, the rise of aftermarket services, and the increasing importance of sustainability in procurement decisions.
The baseline scenario for the global tipper truck market from 2026 to 2035 anticipates steady expansion, underpinned by sustained infrastructure investment, urbanization, and mining activity. Global construction output is expected to grow, particularly in emerging economies, driving demand for rigid and articulated tippers. Mining companies are likely to increase capital expenditure on off-highway dump trucks as commodity demand rises. Regulatory pressures will accelerate the adoption of cleaner powertrains, including electric and hydrogen models, especially in developed markets. The aftermarket segment will gain share as fleets age and require maintenance.
Supply chain constraints, such as steel and semiconductor availability, may pose temporary challenges but are not expected to derail long-term growth. The market index is projected to reach 135 by 2035 (2025=100), corresponding to a CAGR of 3.2%. Asia-Pacific will remain the dominant region, while Latin America and the Middle East & Africa offer untapped potential. Competitive dynamics will intensify, with OEMs focusing on fuel efficiency, telematics, and autonomous features to differentiate.
The construction and demolition sector is the largest end-user of tipper trucks, relying on them for transporting aggregates, sand, gravel, and debris. Demand is closely tied to residential, commercial, and infrastructure construction activity. In 2026, global construction output is expanding, particularly in Asia-Pacific and parts of Africa, driving sales of rigid and articulated tippers. Through 2035, urbanization and population growth will necessitate new housing, roads, and public facilities, sustaining demand. The shift toward modular construction and prefabrication may alter material handling needs but will not reduce overall haulage requirements.
Key demand indicators include construction spending, building permits, and infrastructure project pipelines. The trend toward electric tippers is gaining traction in urban construction due to noise and emissions regulations, but diesel remains dominant in heavy-duty applications. Aftermarket services for these vehicles will grow as fleets expand. Current trend: Growing steadily with infrastructure spending.
Major trends: Increasing adoption of telematics and fleet management systems, Rising demand for electric tippers in urban areas, Growth in rental and leasing services for construction tippers, and Focus on safety features like automatic braking and stability control.
Representative participants: Caterpillar Inc, Volvo Group, Daimler Truck AG, PACCAR Inc, and Tata Motors Limited.
Mining and quarrying operations require heavy-duty off-highway dump trucks capable of hauling large volumes of ore, coal, and minerals. This segment is characterized by high payload capacities and rugged designs. Demand is directly linked to global commodity prices and mining output. As of 2026, mining activity is recovering in key regions like Latin America and Australia, driving replacement and expansion purchases. Through 2035, the energy transition will increase demand for minerals like copper, lithium, and rare earths, boosting off-highway truck sales. Autonomous haulage systems are becoming more prevalent, improving productivity and safety.
Key indicators include mining capital expenditure, commodity price indices, and mine production volumes. The aftermarket for these trucks is significant, with components like tires and hydraulic systems requiring regular replacement. Current trend: Expanding with commodity demand.
Major trends: Rising adoption of autonomous haulage systems, Shift toward electric and hybrid off-highway trucks, Increasing payload capacities for efficiency, and Growth in mining activities in Africa and Latin America.
Representative participants: Caterpillar Inc, Komatsu Ltd, Hitachi Construction Machinery Co., Ltd, Liebherr Group, and Volvo Group.
In agriculture and forestry, tipper trucks are used for transporting grain, feed, timber, and other bulk materials. Demand is driven by mechanization trends and the need for efficient logistics in rural areas. In 2026, emerging economies are investing in agricultural infrastructure, boosting sales of medium-duty tippers. Through 2035, population growth and dietary changes will increase agricultural output, necessitating more haulage capacity. Forestry operations, particularly in North America and Europe, require specialized tippers for timber transport. Key indicators include agricultural production volumes, mechanization rates, and rural road development. The segment is price-sensitive, favoring durable and cost-effective models.
Aftermarket services are crucial due to harsh operating conditions. Current trend: Moderate growth with mechanization.
Major trends: Increasing mechanization in developing countries, Adoption of lightweight materials for higher payloads, Growth in biomass and bioenergy supply chains, and Rising demand for versatile tipper trucks with interchangeable bodies.
Representative participants: Daimler Truck AG, Volvo Group, PACCAR Inc, Tata Motors Limited, and Ashok Leyland Limited.
Waste management services rely on tipper trucks for collecting and transporting municipal solid waste, construction debris, and recyclables. Demand is driven by urbanization, population growth, and stricter environmental regulations. In 2026, cities worldwide are expanding waste collection fleets, with a focus on cleaner technologies. Through 2035, the volume of waste generated will increase, particularly in developing regions, necessitating more tippers. The shift toward recycling and circular economy practices may alter waste streams but will not reduce the need for collection vehicles. Key indicators include municipal waste generation, recycling rates, and government waste management budgets.
Electric tippers are gaining popularity in this segment due to zero tailpipe emissions and lower noise, especially in urban areas. Current trend: Steady growth with urbanization.
Major trends: Adoption of electric and CNG tippers for urban waste collection, Integration of smart waste management systems, Increasing use of compactor tippers for higher efficiency, and Growth in private waste management services.
Representative participants: Volvo Group, Daimler Truck AG, PACCAR Inc, Sinotruk (Hong Kong) Limited, and Dongfeng Motor Corporation.
Road building and landscaping activities require tipper trucks for transporting asphalt, gravel, soil, and other materials. Demand is closely tied to government infrastructure programs and private landscaping projects. In 2026, many countries are investing in road maintenance and expansion, driving sales of articulated and rigid tippers. Through 2035, the need for road connectivity in emerging economies will sustain demand. Landscaping, though smaller, benefits from urbanization and real estate development. Key indicators include road construction expenditure, highway maintenance budgets, and landscaping service demand. The segment favors tippers with high maneuverability and precise dumping capabilities.
Aftermarket services are essential for maintaining uptime. Current trend: Growing with infrastructure projects.
Major trends: Increasing use of GPS and automated controls for precise dumping, Rising demand for articulated tippers for road construction, Growth in road rehabilitation projects in developed markets, and Adoption of low-emission tippers for urban landscaping.
Representative participants: Caterpillar Inc, Volvo Group, Daimler Truck AG, Scania AB, and Ashok Leyland Limited.

articles.summary: South Africa And Egypt Launch Joint Business Council To Boost Trade And Industrial Investment  Trendsnafrica

articles.title: [不同来源] South Africa And Egypt Launch Joint Business Council To Boost Trade And Industrial Investment - Trendsnafrica
articles.summary: South Africa And Egypt Launch Joint Business Council To Boost Trade And Industrial Investment  Trendsnafrica
articles.full_text:
(3 Minutes Read)
South Africa and Egypt have strengthened their economic partnership with the launch of a Joint Business Council (JBC), aimed at expanding bilateral trade, attracting investment and fostering industrial cooperation. The initiative follows a 26% increase in bilateral trade, from 3.4 billion rand in 2024 to 4.3 billion rand in 2025.
The council was officially launched on the sidelines of the Alamein Africa Business Forum in Egypt. It will provide a platform for companies from both countries to identify investment opportunities, establish joint ventures and expand their operations across African and international markets.
According to South Africa’s Department of Trade, Industry and Competition (DTIC), Egypt is a strategic partner and South Africa’s largest export market in North Africa. Its geographical position and industrial base also make it a potential gateway to markets in North Africa, the Middle East and the Horn of Africa.
The council will focus on sectors with significant potential for industrial development and cross-border investment, including automotive manufacturing, mining and mineral beneficiation, agriculture and agri-food processing. Both countries also intend to strengthen cooperation in engineering, infrastructure development, renewable energy and green industries. These partnerships could combine South Africa’s manufacturing capabilities with Egypt’s industrial infrastructure and regional market access, creating opportunities for joint production, technology transfer and expanded distribution networks.
South African exports to Egypt increased by 21%, from 1.3 billion rand in 2024 to 1.6 billion rand in 2025. However, South Africa recorded a trade deficit with Egypt over the 2021–2025 period, highlighting the importance of diversifying exports and expanding commercial opportunities beyond the exchange of goods. The JBC is expected to help address these priorities by encouraging business-to-business partnerships, supporting investment and identifying projects that generate greater local value addition.
A key initiative announced alongside the council’s launch is a proposed joint African investment fund designed to support private-sector businesses and projects with the potential to expand beyond the South African and Egyptian markets. The fund could help mobilise capital for cross-border ventures, support business expansion and strengthen investment links across the continent. However, its proposed size, financing arrangements, governance structure and operational details have not yet been disclosed.
The DTIC said the broader objective is to deepen trade and investment by creating concrete partnerships between companies in both countries, while positioning South Africa and Egypt as gateways to markets across Southern and North Africa and the wider continent.
The council’s launch coincided with the Africa Automotive Investment Forum, attended by South African Minister of Trade, Industry and Competition Parks Tau. Organised in collaboration with Afreximbank and the African Automobile Manufacturers Association (AAAM), the forum focused on attracting investment into Africa’s automotive industry and strengthening regional manufacturing under the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA).
Manufacturers, component suppliers, investors, financial institutions and logistics operators discussed opportunities to expand production capacity, develop integrated supply chains and improve the competitiveness of Africa’s automotive sector. For South Africa, closer cooperation with Egypt could reinforce its position as a major automotive manufacturing hub while opening additional opportunities in North African markets. Egypt, in turn, could benefit from stronger industrial partnerships, expanded manufacturing links and improved access to markets across Southern Africa.
Read Also:
The Joint Business Council reflects a broader effort to translate Africa’s growing commercial opportunities into productive investment, industrial development and stronger regional value chains. By connecting businesses, investors and industry stakeholders, South Africa and Egypt aim to move beyond traditional trading relationships towards joint ventures and projects in manufacturing, mining, agriculture, infrastructure and clean energy. The initiative also supports the wider objectives of the AfCFTA to expand intra-African trade and promote regional industrialisation.
Its success, however, will depend on the implementation of the proposed sectoral initiatives, the mobilisation of investment and the establishment of commercially viable partnerships. With trade between the two economies gaining momentum, the council offers a framework for deepening bilateral relations and strengthening their role in African industrial development. The next challenge will be to turn these ambitions into measurable investment commitments, new production capacity and sustainable business opportunities across the continent.
